title: Disc jockeys, a bebop concert, and meeting Miles Davis
summary: Rose worked with Dave Garroway and Rush Hughes and once produced a bebop concert with Tristano and Fats Navarro. He met Miles Davis at Nat Segal's Downbeat club and thinks he is of no consequence.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: And then when I would go someplace like Chicago or St. Louis, I would work with whoever was the disc jockey that had the jazz audience. And we would co-produce, like Dave Garroway in Chicago or Rush Hughes in St. Louis, that kind of thing. And I worked out a little route, you know, for jazz bands. Uh-huh. And everybody has worked for me. Uh-huh. And there was also even a time when I had a foray into bebop, because there were so many, uh, of the people who were interested in the music that I was producing, that started to talk to me about doing some of the new stuff. And giving the people an opportunity to hear that, because they didn't have any chance to hear that in Philadelphia.

And, uh, the first concert I brought in, in fact, uh, for them, in fact, the only time when I actually ever produced a bebop concert, which I did not produce under my own name, but which featured Lenny Tristano and Fats Navarro and, uh, Billy Bauer and, uh, certain other musicians whose activity was, uh, significant at that time. Uh, you asked about Miles Davis before. Uh-huh. I met Miles Davis in Philadelphia, too. And I met him, uh, there was a, a fellow by the name of Nat Siegel, who was a small, he owned a club called the Downbeat, where these musicians got together and met. And, uh, he invited me over there one time to discuss a major concert, which would include both their kind of music and my kind of music. And Miles Davis was playing in his place that night. And that was the first time that I met him. And, uh, I, as a matter of fact, I had never heard of him before. Uh, I didn't even know what instrument he played. And when, when I sat down at the table with Nat, I didn't even know that he was one of the musicians. But we talked for a while. And then, uh, after having talked for a while, he got up and he played. And I realized that what he was playing was nothing that I could, could produce for my audience.

And I wasn't sure that I wanted, at that time, I wasn't sure that I wanted any identification with it at all. But I was interested to hear what he was doing. And, uh, so when he came back to the table, I talked to him about it again. And, uh, I asked him some questions because I was genuinely curious to know what had led him into this strange approach to music. And I found him to be, uh, literally unable to express himself, uh, verbally. And, uh, uh, after that, I met him other times, you know, because when you're around with musicians, other musicians come in. Uh, I met him a couple of times in Birdland. And I met him in Minton's. Mm-hmm. And I met him, uh, in the Village Vanguard.
And, uh, so when you say hello, you know.
Do you think he's a great musician?
Oh, no. I don't think that he is of really any musical consequence at all.
